tldr: Unlike conventional Real2Sim2Real methods that rely on passive perception from static images, this work combines active camera self-calibration via hand-waving motions with tactile exploration at the fingertips to achieve millimeter-precision fine manipulation on a real humanoid robot.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of ActiveAlign. Offline, 3D assets of scenes and the robot are built using 3DGS and BundleSDF. Online, through an egocentric camera and active motions (hand-waving motions and tactile exploration), the system bridges the gap between the real world and simulation to execute tasks with high precision.
overview:
The Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) framework—where robots plan inside simulation environments and act safely in the real world—has attracted significant attention. However, most existing methods passively perceive scenes using static cameras or single-frame still images. Under this paradigm, calibration errors from egocentric cameras, kinematic compounding errors, and control backlash accumulate together, easily leading to failure in tasks requiring millimeter-level precision such as button pressing or slider adjustments.

To address this, the authors drew inspiration from "active perception," something humans do unconsciously. Humans move their heads to avoid occlusions, wave their hands to gain depth cues, and grope with their fingers to fine-tune the positions of objects. Based on this insight, they propose "ActiveAlign."

ActiveAlign consists of two main modules. The first is "ActiveAlign-Waving," which identifies camera extrinsic parameters online by combining natural hand-waving motions with differentiable rendering. The second is "ActiveAlign-Touching," which generates a local height map by lightly tapping surfaces with fingertips to correct compounding errors from perception and actuation.

In experiments on a real Unitree G1 humanoid robot performing button pressing and slider adjustments, vision-only baselines almost completely failed due to compounding errors, whereas the proposed method achieved high success rates. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that it enables high-precision calibration and simulation reconstruction even on open-source robot datasets with unknown camera parameters.
contributions: Proposing the first end-to-end framework that incorporates the robot's own active motions (hand movements and contact exploration) to bridge the Real2Sim2Real gap.

Developing a differentiable rendering calibration method (ActiveAlign-Waving) that solves the ill-posed problem inherent to articulated humanoids using importance sampling and active multi-pose motions.

Proposing contact alignment (ActiveAlign-Touching) that quickly constructs a local height map on a 2D surface via touch to cancel millimeter-scale compounding errors without heavy 3D surface reconstruction.
Demonstrating effectiveness both in fine manipulation of switches, sliders, and similar objects using a real Unitree G1 robot, and in automatic calibration of open-source manipulation datasets.

sections.heading: Why Do Robots Need to "Wave and Touch"?
sections.summary: To act safely in the real world, precise alignment between simulation and reality is essential, yet passive perception from static images cannot eliminate millimeter-level errors. This work proposes ActiveAlign, which fundamentally resolves this alignment problem by actively moving the body and exploring with touch like humans do.
sections.details:
When robots perform tasks in real environments, accurately discovering, tracking, and aligning objects determines success or failure. In fine manipulation such as pressing buttons or moving sliders, a discrepancy of just a few millimeters leads to catastrophic failure.

To address this challenge, researchers have explored Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) to build structured simulation assets from the real world for safe planning. However, many existing methods lean toward "passive perception." That is, because they attempt to create simulations based on imperfect observations obtained from stationary viewpoints, they cannot actively close the divergence between reality and simulation (the Real2Sim gap).

Here, the authors focused on human behavioral patterns. Humans tilt their heads or move their hands to gauge depth, and when pressing a tiny switch, they roughly aim visually and then touch with their fingertips to verify the position. Bringing this same concept into egocentric robot manipulation is the core idea of this paper.

Specifically, the authors introduce "ActiveAlign-Waving," which optimizes camera parameters online via hand-waving motions and differentiable rendering, and "ActiveAlign-Touching," which eliminates millimeter-level discrepancies via fingertip touch, aligning the real world and simulation in a fully end-to-end manner.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of ActiveAlign. It illustrates the pipeline of offline object and robot reconstruction, alongside online egocentric camera calibration (Waving) and contact refinement using tactile height maps (Touching).

sections.heading: Waving to Align the Camera, Touching to Erase Millimeter Errors
sections.summary: The method consists of offline asset construction and online real-time execution. Online, it calibrates camera pose via differentiable rendering that leverages waving motions and importance sampling, and cancels compounding errors by creating a local height map through fingertip tactile exploration.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Pipeline Foundations and Errors Encountered
ActiveAlign operates in two stages: an offline phase and an online phase. Offline, it builds 3D models of scenes and objects from multi-frame RGB-D images using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and BundleSDF. Online, it discovers and segments objects using GroundingDINO and SAM2, estimates poses with FoundationPose, and synchronizes real-world states into simulation in real time.

However, two deep-rooted errors remain in this baseline: (1) calibration errors from markerless egocentric cameras, and (2) "compounding errors" where perception errors stack on top of the humanoid's long kinematic chains, backlash, and control errors. Active perception is used to solve both.

### 2.2 ActiveAlign-Waving: Online Camera Calibration via Active Motion
To automatically calibrate camera extrinsic parameters $T_{base\to cam}$, the authors adopted differentiable rendering based on 3DGS. By incorporating mesh deformation according to robot joint angles $\bm{p}$ into 3DGS, they optimize camera parameters to minimize the discrepancy between rendered depth images and real-robot depth images $D$.

However, in high-DOF humanoids equipped with an egocentric camera, only the hands appear in the field of view and the degree of freedom is excessively high, making the optimization prone to local minima. They introduced two key ideas:
- Importance sampling: Rather than uniformly sampling joint space, they sample with emphasis based on the geometric prior that "the camera is looking at both hands during manipulation," pre-training a degradation-free 3DGS model.
- Active perception (hand-waving motions): Rather than relying on a single image, the robot acquires multiple frames from a sequence where it actively waves its hands (or stationary intervals within motion trajectories) and optimizes camera parameters to satisfy them simultaneously. This enables remarkably stable calibration even from an egocentric perspective.

### 2.3 ActiveAlign-Touching: Fine Alignment via Tactile Feedback
Even if visual pose estimation is highly accurate, when the robot extends its fingertips toward the target, compounding errors cause it to miss by several millimeters. Thus, the system mimics how humans feel around for a switch.

Because performing full 3D shape reconstruction via touch takes too much time, this method treats the manipulation surface as a 2D plane and constructs a "local height map" along the $z$-direction. Around the visually identified region of interest (e.g., the center of a slider knob), the fingertip densely taps while slowly descending until reaching a constant contact force threshold $T_{\text{force}}$. By directly mapping the resulting height map to the robot's action space, fine manipulation completely absorbs discrepancies between perception and actuation.

sections.heading: Proving the Power on a Real Humanoid and Public Datasets
sections.summary: In fine manipulation experiments using a real Unitree G1, introducing tactile alignment dramatically improved the success rate of model-based planning. Furthermore, across multiple public robot datasets lacking calibration data, the waving approach demonstrated accurate and consistent camera calibration.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
To validate camera calibration, the authors used both simulation (with added lighting variations and initial value noise) and a real robot. The real robot was a Unitree G1 equipped with a ZED Mini stereo camera on its head (with a Dynamixel motor for neck pan/tilt) and Alt-Bionics Surge hands or Dex3 hands fitted with SensibleRobotics RoboSkin tactile sensors (an 80-element array) at the fingertips. For evaluating fine manipulation, three types of panels requiring millimeter-level precision were prepared, including DJ controller sliders and wall switches.

### 3.1 Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation: Touch Breaks the Millimeter Barrier
Even with visual Real2Sim and camera calibration completed, while coarse tasks like grasping bottles were possible, model-based trajectory planning baselines yielded very low success rates on button pressing and slider manipulation. The culprit was compounding errors spanning from perception to control.

In contrast, when tactile alignment (ActiveAlign-Touching) was introduced to construct local height maps, success rates improved significantly across all target objects. The two-stage approach—coarse approach via vision, followed by tactile mapping to correct millimeter-scale discrepancies between the actuation point and protrusion positions—proved to play a decisive role in real-robot manipulation.

### 3.2 Real2Sim Generalizability on Public Datasets
To verify whether the proposed camera calibration (ActiveAlign-Waving) generalizes beyond their own platform, the authors applied it to public datasets without camera calibration information (xdof, Mobile ALOHA, Humanoid Everyday). Stationary intervals were automatically extracted from robot trajectory logs as active motion observations for optimization.

As a result, it consistently recorded higher IoU (measuring the overlap between real-robot masks and rendered masks) than conventional single-frame optimization methods. Variance in estimated camera poses across episodes was also substantially suppressed, demonstrating practical utility in automatically constructing high-fidelity simulation environments from large amounts of existing uncalibrated data.

captions.F4: Real2Sim reproduction results on uncalibrated public robot datasets (such as Mobile ALOHA and Humanoid Everyday). Through ActiveAlign-Waving, camera poses and hand positions in real-world images (top) match simulations (bottom) remarkably well.

sections.heading: Active Perception Unlocks High-Precision Real2Sim2Real
sections.summary: ActiveAlign was proposed to bridge the Real2Sim2Real gap by leveraging active perception. Its efficacy was established in both high-fidelity simulation environment generation from public datasets and millimeter-scale fine manipulation on a real Unitree G1.
sections.details:
This paper proposed ActiveAlign, a framework that overcomes the limitations of conventional passive approaches based on static images and seamlessly connects reality with simulation via active perception.

Camera calibration using active hand motions (ActiveAlign-Waving) enabled robust pose estimation even for humanoids equipped only with egocentric cameras and for uncalibrated public datasets. Furthermore, contact surface alignment via tactile exploration (ActiveAlign-Touching) cancels out compounding errors emerging along the perception-calibration-control chain through physical contact feedback, achieving millimeter-precision switch operations on a real humanoid.

The active perception paradigm—where robots actively move their own bodies to elicit information and self-correct—is expected to become an indispensable foundational technology in future general-purpose humanoid manipulation.

sections.heading: Appendix: Hardware Setup and the Secret Behind Importance Sampling
sections.summary: This section covers the computational setup running the entire pipeline in real time on an onboard Jetson AGX Orin, as well as why importance sampling is essential when pre-training 3DGS models for humanoids.
sections.details:
### Computational System and Hardware Setup
For onboard computation, the robot employs an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin (64GB) capable of running on battery power at 75W. The robot's control signal update and state synchronization threads run at 60Hz. Object detection and segmentation (GroundingDINO and SAM2) run at startup (and on periodic calls as needed). The pose estimator, FoundationPose, runs stably at 2 FPS on the Orin while coordinating with other concurrent threads.

### Why Is Importance Sampling Necessary?
Prior work (such as DRRobot) trained rendering 3DGS models by uniformly sampling the robot's joint angle space. While this works for a single robot arm, uniform sampling on a full-body humanoid like the Unitree G1—which has 29 body DOFs and 14 hand DOFs—leads to frequent self-occlusions due to joint combinations, producing extremely unnatural poses in training images.

Consequently, parts of the 3DGS model used for optimization degrade, preventing camera calibration optimization from converging. By applying conditional importance sampling based on "the camera is looking at the hands," an intact 3DGS model can be constructed, achieving stable camera extrinsic parameter optimization.

captions.F5: Sequential photographs showing the robot naturally waving its hands during ActiveAlign-Waving. By moving its hands like a human to obtain multi-view observations, it prevents differentiable rendering camera parameter optimization from falling into local minima.

takeaways: Creating an active "move, touch, and verify" loop resolves millimeter-scale compounding errors far more robustly than striving for "high-precision passive perception."
For markerless calibration of egocentric humanoids, relying on geometric constraints across multiple frames via active hand-waving motions is far more effective than depending on single frames.
Tactile shape refinement does not need to aim for complete 3D reconstruction; treating target surfaces as 2D planes to build local height maps is fast and sufficiently practical.
Even on uncalibrated public robot manipulation datasets, stationary intervals in trajectories can be treated as active observations to retroactively convert them into high-fidelity simulation assets.
limitations: Tactile exploration (ActiveAlign-Touching) assumes protruding objects like switches and sliders situated on planar surfaces; its applicability to objects with complex 3D freeform surfaces has not been verified.
Constructing tactile height maps requires extra exploration time for tapping local areas with fingertips, introducing a trade-off with the overall immediacy of task execution.

In situations where arms move so broadly that head cameras cannot capture the hands, or when operating outside the field of view, the geometric constraints of ActiveAlign-Waving become difficult to satisfy.
